hero.name: Merijn Kersten
hero.subheading: I make things you can walk around, pick up and play with.

intro.title: Hi, I’m Merijn
intro.body: and this is my work in miniature.

capabilitiesIntro.title: The three scales I work at
capabilitiesIntro.lead: A city, a room and a chip. Most projects need all three, and I like being the one who connects them.

workIntro.title: Chronology
workIntro.lead: From shaders to screws: a bunch of projects from over the years. Some ended up on millions of phones, a few went straight onto the shelf. They’re all in here, in order.

career.blurb: Where it started: an internship at a 3D agency, which turned into a job building VR and standing next to it at trade fairs. I also built the office PCs, because someone had to.
career.detail: My career started at Letink Design, where I built VR and AR applications for construction, tourism and government clients, published them online and supported clients on site at trade fairs and events. I also made explainer animations, built interactive installations and put together the office PCs.

career.blurb: A development studio in Amsterdam. I came in as an intern, worked on games and XR, and ended up helping to lead the team. This is where I found out I’d picked the right job.
career.detail: I started at DTT as an intern and ended up helping to lead a team of developers on VR, Android, iOS and web projects. I helped select and mentor new developers, improved how the team worked, and built features such as deep linking, iOS plugins, XR, multiplayer, in-app purchases and optimisation.

career.blurb: AR seek-and-find and audiobook apps for children’s books, which I designed, built and published on my own. I found out that the last 10% (support, store reviews, odd feedback) is most of the work.
career.detail: As a freelancer for the publisher Zwijsen I built AR seek-and-find and audiobook apps for children’s books. I did all of it myself: design, development, testing and publishing to the stores. The apps open from a QR code in the book and have been downloaded tens of thousands of times, with only positive reviews.

career.blurb: Casual mobile games for a very large audience. They’re on millions of phones and have to stay fun and stable for a long time, which is harder than it sounds. I’ve never learnt as fast as I did here.
career.detail: I joined Popcore to build hyper-casual games for a very large Android and iOS audience. I ran live-ops on titles like Parking Jam, Pull the Pin and Wrecking Ball, and built new game modes, multiplayer features and tools for editors and level designers, all on an ECS framework for speed and flexibility. It’s where I grew fastest as a developer.

career.blurb: Wonderment pins AR to real places and tells stories there. The one I’m proudest of is a tour I came up with about the Market Garden landings, which happened where I was born. I really wanted to help tell that one.
career.detail: I joined Wonderment because I wanted to do more AR, and built location-based work there: visualisations, games and web applications, plus R&D into image recognition with machine learning in Unity and Lens Studio. Most of my time went into VPS and Cesium, which pin AR to the outside world with centimetre accuracy, and into enriching places with geodata such as GIS, 3D map tiles and GeoJSON. I’m proudest of leading the development of a multiplayer racing game and a photo installation for Niantic.

career.blurb: The consultancy my recent jobs run through. Philips, Alliander and the Marechaussee all came via Rebels, so I’ve been moving between health care, energy and defence. Each has its own rules, especially about what I’m allowed to install.
career.detail: Rebels is the consultancy my recent assignments run through. Philips’ immersive lab, Alliander and the Royal Netherlands Marechaussee were all placements through them, so I’ve moved between health care, energy and defence: several clients in a short time, each worth getting to know from the inside.

career.blurb: XR and AI prototypes at Philips’ immersive lab, trying to get new spatial tech to the point where a hospital can rely on it. A lot of research turns out to be finding what isn’t worth building, and it’s better to find that out early.
career.detail: At Philips’ immersive lab I visualised medical equipment such as CT scanners, and new procedures. I built VR applications that introduce people to new medical developments, for education and for presenting at trade fairs.

career.blurb: In a small team we built a HoloLens prototype that shows a transformer station on the real street before it’s built. It worked. If it had been up to me, it would have run on an iPad.
career.detail: At Alliander I worked in a small team on HoloLens software that shows field crews information from the grid database in the place it belongs to, to make building medium-voltage stations more efficient. I was responsible for the development, optimisation and UX of these apps, and also worked on visualising whole neighbourhoods from 3D scans.

career.blurb: Back at the immersive lab, this time in Unreal, making digital humans whose faces change colour with their heartbeat. We used them to train AI to read a pulse from video, across a wider range of skin types.
career.detail: Back at the immersive lab we worked from research papers to build the first Unreal MetaHumans whose skin colour changes realistically with their heartbeat. They generate synthetic data for training AI models to detect a heartbeat from a distance, more accurately and across more skin types.

career.blurb: At the Dutch military police I’m connecting VR players inside a training simulation that’s been in development for years. The security is what you’d expect, so I’ve built most of the networking myself.
career.detail: For the Dutch military police I connect VR players inside a complex training system that has been in development for years. Because of the security requirements I built many of the networking components myself, and learnt how they work in detail.

about.title: About the artist
about.lead: Hi, I’m Merijn. I live in Utrecht, and for about ten years I’ve been building *AR and VR*: things that aren’t there, for people who are. I love the technology, but what I’m really after is the moment someone stops noticing it.
body: I think software is a theory until somebody uses it. So I stay with a project until it’s in use, close enough to watch the theory fail and fix it quickly. For ARCam that meant flying out to set the installations up myself, and spending a day in a city I didn’t know looking for one type of screw. Reality has more edge cases than any test plan, and it’s usually right. I’d rather hear early that something doesn’t work than find out at the end, and I do my best thinking with colleagues who don’t mind being wrong out loud.

Every system is a guess about the future. For my graduation I made a large one: a framework on top of Apple’s ARKit and Google’s ARCore, so an iPhone and an Android phone could look at the same table and agree on what was on it. It worked, it was too clever for anyone else to maintain, and then Unity released the same idea done properly. Being made unnecessary turned out to be a compliment. It’s also where I fell for this kind of programming: a puzzle that breaks every day, and some mornings I wake up with the answer.

You only notice a detail when it’s wrong. I learnt that in Berlin, making mobile games at a studio where I was, at first, a bit underqualified. More than twenty games later I know that whether something feels right is decided in places nobody can point to: how long an animation takes, the pause before a reward, a control that does what your thumb had already assumed. Nobody thanks you for getting these right. They just keep playing, which I’ve decided to take as thanks.

Right now I’m connecting VR players for the Dutch military police. I’m more of a nerd than a soldier and never expected to work at a barracks. I’m there as a consultant through Rebels, and security is tight enough that I wrote most of the networking myself. Before that I was at Philips’ immersive lab. Meanwhile AI is changing how I work faster than I can form an opinion about it. It has made me more productive and less certain, which seems about right. If you like thinking about what technology is for as much as what it can do, I’d like to hear from you.
